column3: Close to the Hebrew.
Close to the Hebrew.
Close to the Hebrew.
Explicitly apportions the lamb according to each person’s eating, rather than leaving this as “accordingly.”
Retains the age expression “a son of a year.”
“Slaughter it” has a singular object rather than “slaughter the animals”; the time is “between the two evenings.”
Names the two doorposts and the lintel, rather than the sides and tops of doorframes.
Close to the Hebrew.
Close to the Hebrew.
What remains until morning is to be burned with fire; the wording does not add “before the morning.”
“Your loins girded” retains the bodily image rather than “fully dressed for travel.”
Says “every firstborn,” without a separate adjective “male.”
The blood is “a sign for you,” rather than simply distinguishing the houses.
Repeats the command to celebrate the day after describing the perpetual statute.
Close to the Hebrew.
The exception is expressed as “that which is eaten by every person,” rather than explicitly “prepare the meals.”
Says to keep the unleavened bread, without an explicit word “Feast.”

Close to the Hebrew.
Retains the two actions “draw out and take,” rather than “Go at once and select.”
Repeats “the blood which is in the basin” and explicitly names the lintel and two doorposts.
Names the LORD again as the subject of passing over the doorway, rather than continuing only with pronouns.
Names “your sons,” rather than the broader “your descendants.”
Close to the Hebrew.
Close to the Hebrew.
Retains the two bodily actions of bowing low and prostrating themselves, rather than describing the second only as worship.
Repeats “they did” after naming what the LORD commanded Moses and Aaron.
“The house of the pit” retains the compound image rendered “the dungeon”; no separate adjective “male” is added to the firstborn.
Calls Pharaoh’s attendants his servants rather than his officials.
